issues.description: Fixed-packet send loop blocks the writer with an unbounded inner while
issues.detail: When fixed_audio_packet_size is small relative to incoming payloads, a single _write_frame call can issue many sequential awaits inside the loop without yielding control elsewhere. A simple data shape change helps: compute n = len(buf) // packet_bytes once, slice off n*packet_bytes, then iterate. Even better, make the chunker a stateless filter function (buffer, size) -> (chunks, remainder) so it can be unit-tested without the transport. The current code mixes buffering, slicing, and I/O in one method.

issues.description: Packetization belongs in the serializer, not the transport
issues.detail: The transport now knows about PCM packet sizes, which is a serializer/protocol concern. Vonage requires fixed framing; that fact lives in vonage.py's docstring but the enforcement lives in fastapi.py. This is the wrong data shape: the serializer should emit a stream of correctly-sized chunks (an iterable/generator of bytes), and the transport should just send whatever comes out. That removes the buffer-state from the transport entirely, makes the serializer self-contained, and means any future protocol-framed serializer (Twilio, Plivo, etc.) doesn't need transport changes. Classic 'data structures, not classes' move: change serialize() return shape from `bytes | str | None` to allow `Iterable[bytes | str]`, and the algorithm becomes self-evident.

issues.description: DTMF digit lookup hedges two shapes without committing to one
issues.detail: `digit = message.get("digit") or message.get("dtmf", {}).get("digit")` tries two shapes because the author wasn't sure which Vonage sends. Pick one based on the documented protocol; if both are real, document why and which takes precedence. Speculative fallback code rots — a year from now no one will know whether the second branch is still needed.

issues.description: deserialize event dispatch is a small if/elif chain that wants a dict
issues.detail: The text-event handling is six branches that all just log and return None except the DTMF case. A small dict mapping event name to handler function would make the data shape obvious and let the DTMF case stand out as the only one doing real work. Minor — but the current shape hides the one branch that matters among five that don't.

Both serialize() and deserialize() do `if resampled is None or len(resampled) == 0: return None`. Small duplication, but it's a hint that the resampler return contract is awkward — callers shouldn't have to check two ways for 'no audio'. Either the resampler should return `b''` consistently (then one check suffices) or callers should wrap it. Not load-bearing; flag for cleanup.

The InterruptionFrame handler now has to know about fixed_audio_packet_size to clear the buffer. If packetization lived in the serializer (see P1 above), the serializer could handle its own reset via setup/interruption hooks, and the transport would stay ignorant. As written, every future state added to the transport's audio pipeline will need a matching clear here — a maintenance trap.

review.summary: The Vonage serializer is small, readable, and mostly does one thing well — good filter shape on the deserialize side. The real design issue is in fastapi.py: protocol-level packetization is leaking into the transport, where it doesn't belong. Vonage requires 20ms fixed PCM frames; that's a Vonage protocol fact, so the Vonage serializer (or any framed serializer) should emit a stream of correctly-sized chunks and the transport should stay dumb. Changing the serialize() return shape from `bytes | str | None` to also allow `Iterable[bytes | str]` would let every protocol-framed serializer compose naturally and would delete the buffer state, the interruption-clear coupling, and the `fixed_audio_packet_size` parameter entirely. Smaller nits: a couple of duplicated empty-payload checks, a hedged DTMF digit lookup, and an event dispatch that wants to be a dict.
